title: Why Good Teams Surface Risk Early (Without the Panic)
summary: Hidden risk only gets more expensive. How good teams name risks early, write them so they can be tested, run a premortem and react so people keep speaking up.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Wednesday standup, two weeks before launch. Every update sounds fine. Privately, though, three people are each sitting on a worry. The payment provider's sandbox doesn't behave the way its docs say. The data migration turned out bigger than the estimate once someone actually counted rows. The test data looks nothing like production. Nobody mentions any of it, because nobody wants to be the first to make the plan sound shaky. So the status stays green.

That green is the most expensive color on the board. A risk named today still leaves room to cut scope, reorder the work, add a test, change the rollout or warn stakeholders. The same risk found the night before launch leaves one option: hope.

Why people sit on risks

People rarely hide a risk because they don't care. They hide it because speaking up feels costly now and the payoff feels far away. Saying "I found a risk" before you have a fix can sound like you're not on top of your work.

Blame makes that cost higher. In Strategies for Learning from Failure, Amy Edmondson describes asking executives how many of the failures in their organizations are truly blameworthy. The answers are usually 2 to 5 percent. Asked how many are treated as blameworthy, they say 70 to 90 percent. If most problems get handled as someone's fault, it's no surprise people say nothing until a problem can't be denied.

You can hear a team's risk culture in small phrases. Do people say "I found a risk", or do they wait until they can say "I found the fix"? Does the lead treat an early warning as useful information or as a lack of confidence? Does the room slow down to understand the signal, or rush to defend the plan?

A useful risk note is specific

Making a risk visible isn't the same as making it dramatic. "I'm worried about performance" gives the team nothing to do. Compare these:

  • "The import job may hit the worker timeout for accounts with very long histories. We haven't tested anything bigger than the staging data."
  • "The provider's callback isn't idempotent in the sandbox. If they retry, we could charge a customer twice."
  • "The old app version still reads the field we're removing. Anyone who hasn't updated will get a blank screen."

Each one gives the team something to test, contain or accept on purpose. A simple format works in a channel or a ticket: what might happen, how likely it looks, what it would cost, the next check and who owns that check.

Risk: provider callback isn't idempotent in sandbox
If it happens: a retry could charge a customer twice
Likelihood: unclear; sandbox retried twice this week
Next check: replay a callback on staging (Thu)
Owner: payments on-call
Decide by: Friday planning

Run a premortem before the plan sets

One of the easiest ways to drag risks into the open is Gary Klein's premortem (Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review, 2007). A postmortem asks what went wrong after the fact. A premortem asks the team to assume the project has already failed and work out why. The steps, as Klein lays them out:

  1. Brief the team on the plan.
  2. The lead says: imagine it's some months from now and this project has failed spectacularly.
  3. Everyone writes down, on their own, every reason they can think of for the failure.
  4. Go round the room, starting with the project lead, one reason per person per turn, until every reason is on the list.
  5. The project lead uses the list to strengthen the plan.

Two details make it work. Writing alone first means people don't simply echo the most senior voice. And because everyone has been asked to find reasons for failure, raising a worry becomes the assignment, so nobody looks disloyal for doing it. Klein's own framing is that the exercise makes it safe for knowledgeable people who are worried about a project's weak spots to speak up. He also points to 1989 research on "prospective hindsight": imagining that an event has already happened makes it easier to come up with reasons for it.

How you react decides whether they tell you next time

The first time someone raises a risk, the whole team watches what happens to them. If every risk turns into blame, people hide risks until they're undeniable. If every risk turns into panic, people stop telling small concerns apart from real blockers. What works is curiosity plus three short questions: What evidence do we have? What can we do this week? Who else needs to know?

Then thank the person in public, especially when the risk turns out to be nothing. An early false alarm is cheap. A team that stops raising alarms is very expensive.

Early risk also protects trust with stakeholders. Most people take an uncomfortable truth better than a late surprise. A team that reports risk early can sound less certain in the moment. Over time it becomes the team others can plan around: green means green, yellow means yellow, and silence doesn't mean something is being hidden.

The same thinking belongs in a rollout plan. When we rolled out PC message backup on Zalo PC, the plan listed the known risks before the first wave, risky changes shipped switched off behind remote kill switches, and monitoring was in place from the start. None of that made the risks go away. It meant that if one did show up, someone would already be watching and could turn the change off without shipping a new build.

Visibility should lead to action

A board covered in red sticky notes doesn't prove maturity on its own. Every visible risk needs a next check, an owner and a date when someone decides. Some risks get accepted with eyes open. Some get retired once a test shows they won't happen. Some change the plan. The point is to keep the work steerable. When a risk becomes a reason to pause a release, how to say "not yet" without becoming the blocker covers the next step. If it turns into an incident anyway, a blameless postmortem keeps people telling the truth.

Try this week

  • At your next standup, ask "what's one thing that could make this slip?" and actually wait for an answer.
  • Turn one vague worry into a risk note with a next check and an owner.
  • Run a 30-minute premortem before your next project kicks off.
  • Thank the next person who raises a risk, even if it turns out to be nothing.

faqs.q: Why should teams surface risks early?
faqs.a: Because the options shrink as the deadline gets closer. A risk named early still leaves room to cut scope, reorder work, add a test, change the rollout or warn stakeholders. The same risk found the night before launch leaves almost nothing to do except hope.

A technique described by Gary Klein in Harvard Business Review in 2007. The team imagines the project has already failed, each person writes down every reason they can think of on their own, the group goes round sharing one reason at a time, and the project lead uses the list to strengthen the plan.

faqs.q: How do you write a useful risk note?
faqs.a: Make it specific enough to test: what might happen, how likely it looks, what it would cost, the next check and who owns it, plus a date for the decision. "The callback isn't idempotent in sandbox, so a retry could charge twice" is useful. "I'm worried about payments" isn't.

faqs.q: Why do people hide risks at work?
faqs.a: Speaking up feels costly and the payoff feels distant, and blame raises the cost. Amy Edmondson reports that executives she asks usually estimate only 2 to 5 percent of failures in their organizations are truly blameworthy, yet say 70 to 90 percent are treated that way.

faqs.q: How should a team lead respond when someone raises a risk?
faqs.a: With curiosity: ask what evidence there is, what the team can do this week and who else needs to know. Thank the person publicly, even when the risk turns out to be nothing, and make sure every visible risk gets an owner, a next check and a decision date.
